The ABCD of Active Communities
Alex Johnson, community organizer
Communities have traditionally been groups of people with common
interests who
live near one another.
As people focus more on online
connections, involving people in their local communities has become difficult.
The ABCD (Asset-Based
'
Community Development) model helps with
this
problem by focusing on a community's assets - or resources - rather
than what
it is missing.
By encouraging everyone to look at their individual
strengths, communities can manage their own growth and find lasting
solutions.
The community assets can be grouped into five different categories.
People themselves make up the first asset.
Individuals have unique skills
and experiences that can help the community.
For example, a carpenter might
help repair public spaces・When
a community recognizes and benefits from
the strengths of its members,
it creates a sense of pride and belon9in9.
This
encourages more people to work together on projects useful for all.
The second asset is associations.
These are groups of people who come
together
to share a common interest or purpose, such as sports clubs or
cultural groups.
Associations often have strong networks that can be used to
organize community projects.
The third key asset
is local institutions, such as schools and businesses.
As they offer services and jobs
to the community,
the success
of the
community depends on them.
One local business might sponsor a community
event or provide space fOr meetings.
Working with institutions ensures that
communities can get the resources they need.
Location-based assets!
like parks, buildings, roads, and lands, form the
fourth asset.
These spaces and cultural activities together help shape the
community's identity.
They give people places to gather and strengthen their
－③－16-

sense of belonging.
Finally, exchange or interaction - the relationships between the local
economy and the people -
is a key asset for a strong community.
These
connections make the community richer, build trust and make
it easier for
resources or information to be shared.
Strong social ties ensure that everyone
feels included and can work together to solve problems.
